Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
First, intellectual developments do not appear suddenly and spontaneously without earlier developments preparing the way for them.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Second, intellectual developments do not arise apart from social developments. They are connected to them in one way or another, sometimes directly and sometimes indirectly.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Third, as we will soon see, the debate over divine decree in particular was connected to a position that was political in substance even though it appeared in religious form.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Once we take these three points into account, we have good reason to reject the common claim made by many historians of Arab philosophy that discussion of this problem began with Maʿbad al-Juhanī.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
There is another historical reason for rejecting that claim.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

It is well known that the Sunnis regarded ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib as the first of their theologians. They say that he debated the Kharijites over God’s promise and threat, and debated the Qadarites over divine will and human power. Here “divine will” means God’s will, while “human power” means a person’s ability to act by choice.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

It is also reported that ʿAlī himself knew of a well-known Qadarite in the time of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb named ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṣayfī, who argued about divine decree. ʿAlī is said to have reported how ʿUmar prevented ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṣayfī from publicly arguing for his view.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
This would mean that the issue was already being raised in the time of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

There is even reason to think that it had been raised during the Prophet’s lifetime. We may recall what we discussed in Chapter Two of Part One: the Prophet was said to become extremely angry when he heard people arguing—that is, arguing about divine decree.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
We also have a report attributed to the Prophet:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
“No people went astray after having been rightly guided except that they were given to argument.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Much of the argument referred to in this report, as well as in other reports mentioned in that earlier chapter, concerned questions such as the relationship between divine decree and human will and action.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Muslim historians have also preserved examples of debates over this very question during the time of the Rightly Guided Caliphs. Here are two of them.

They report that a man came to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib and asked:

“Commander of the Faithful, tell me about divine decree.”

ʿAlī replied: “It is a narrow path. Do not walk it.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
But the man did not stop. He said again: “Commander of the Faithful, tell me about divine decree.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
ʿAlī replied: “It is a deep sea. Do not enter it.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
The man was still not satisfied. Once again he asked: “Commander of the Faithful, tell me about divine decree.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
ʿAlī replied: “It is a hidden secret of God. Do not uncover it.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
The man again said: “Commander of the Faithful, tell me about divine decree.”

ʿAlī then asked him: “Did God create you as He wished, or as you wished?”

ʿAlī asked: “And on the Day of Resurrection, will God raise you as you wish or as He wishes?”

ʿAlī then said: “Do you possess a will alongside God’s will, above His will, or below His will? If you say that your will exists alongside His, you claim to share His authority. If you say that it exists below His will, you claim that you can do without His will. And if you say that it is above His will, then your will would overpower His.”

Then ʿAlī asked: “Do you not ask God for well-being?”

ʿAlī asked: “From what do you ask Him to protect you? From an affliction He has placed upon you, or from an affliction placed upon you by someone else?”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
The man answered: “From an affliction He has placed upon me.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
ʿAlī said: “Do you not say, ‘There is no power and no strength except through God, the Most High, the Almighty’?”

ʿAlī asked: “Do you know what that means?”

The man said: “No, Commander of the Faithful. Teach me from what God has taught you.”

ʿAlī replied: “It means that a servant has no power to obey God and no power to disobey Him except through God Almighty. Questioner, God makes people ill and He heals them. From Him comes the illness and from Him comes the cure. Understand this from God.”

ʿAlī said to him: “Then have you now become a Muslim? Stand up and take the hand of your Muslim brother.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
ʿAlī then said: “If I found a man from among the Qadarites, I would seize him by the neck and keep striking him until I broke it. They are the Jews of this community.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Another report, also attributed to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, tells the story differently:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
“When ʿAlī returned from Ṣiffīn, one of his followers stood up and asked him: ‘Tell us about our journey from Syria. Was it by divine decree and predestination?’
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
“ʿAlī replied: ‘By Him who split the seed and created life, we did not descend into a valley or climb a hill except by divine decree and predestination.’
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
“The man said: ‘Then I leave my hardship with God’—meaning that his effort had been wasted—‘and I have no reward for it.’
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

“ʿAlī replied: ‘On the contrary, old man. May God greatly reward you for your journey while you were travelling and for your rest while you were resting. In none of these situations were you forced or compelled.’
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
“The man said: ‘But how can that be, if divine decree and predestination drove us and our journey came from them?’
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

“ʿAlī replied: ‘Perhaps you think that divine decree means an unavoidable command and predestination an inescapable fate. If that were so, reward and punishment would become meaningless, God’s promise and threat would have no purpose, no sinner could be blamed and no good person praised. The person who did good would have no greater claim to reward than the person who did evil, and the person who did evil would have no greater claim to punishment than the person who did good.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
“‘That is the teaching of devils, idol worshippers, enemies of the Merciful, false witnesses, and those blind to what is right. They are the Qadarites of this community and its Magians.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

“‘God commanded while leaving people a choice, and He prohibited as a warning. He did not impose duties on people while compelling them, nor did He send the prophets in vain. That is what those who disbelieve imagine, and woe to those who disbelieve because of the Fire.’
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
“The man asked: ‘Then what are the divine decree and predestination that led us here?’

Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
“Then he recited: ‘Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and that you show kindness to your parents.’”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
There is an obvious difference between ʿAlī’s answer in these two reports.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
In the first, he seems to affirm absolute compulsion. In the second, he interprets divine decree and predestination in a way that rejects absolute compulsion and leaves room for human choice.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
This difference gives us reason to doubt whether both reports really go back to ʿAlī himself.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

But our main concern here is not to investigate the authenticity of the reports. What matters more is what they show us about the history of the question: people were already thinking about divine decree in the period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs. The uncertainty surrounding the problem troubled them, and they tried to overcome that uncertainty by asking questions, pressing for answers, and debating the issue.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Our doubts about whether these two reports can really be attributed to ʿAlī do not make us doubt that they arose out of the period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs. The style of the questions and answers, and the way the issue itself is expressed, seem to us to belong to that period.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Even so, the first report appears more likely than the second to preserve something genuinely connected to ʿAlī. The wording of the second almost seems to have been composed according to the later Qadarite interpretation of divine decree, after the period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Those who created the report seem to have tried hard to make it fit not only the language of that earlier period but also its historical events. That is why the story is placed specifically in the context of the Battle of Ṣiffīn.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
In any case, despite the obvious signs of later invention, the report still has historical value.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

By this we mean that it supports what many other sources also show: debate over this question was common during the period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, and people were eager to know what those caliphs thought about the effect of divine decree and predestination on their lives and on the consequences of their actions.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
There is another piece of evidence that gives even stronger support to our account of the historical setting of the problem.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Aḥmad Amīn quotes Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā al-Murtaḍā, author of al-Munya wa-l-Amal fī Sharḥ Kitāb al-Milal wa-l-Niḥal, as saying that Muʿtazilism goes back to the earliest period of Islam.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Al-Murtaḍā places the four caliphs, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd, and others in the first generation of Muʿtazilites. In the second generation he places al-Ḥasan, al-Ḥusayn, Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyya, Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, and others. In the third he includes al-Ḥasan ibn al-Ḥasan, ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥasan, and Abū Hāshim ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyya, from whom Wāṣil is said to have learned. In the fourth he places Ghaylān al-Dimashqī, Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ, and others.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

“What appears from his words is that he wants to count as a Muʿtazilite anyone among the Companions or Followers from whom a statement has been reported showing either that human beings possess freedom of will or that moral good and evil can be known by reason.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

“For example, Ibn al-Murtaḍā argues that Abū Bakr and Ibn Masʿūd held the Muʿtazilite position because, in the case of a woman whose marriage contract left her dowry unspecified, they gave judgment according to their own reasoning. In other words, he takes this as evidence that they believed moral good and evil could be known rationally.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
“He also argues that Ibn ʿAbbās held this position because he debated the Syrian supporters of compulsion and defeated their argument.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
“Ibn al-Murtaḍā does not mean that Muʿtazilism, under that name and as a fully formed school, already existed in the time of Abū Bakr.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

The conclusion we draw from all this historical evidence is the point we have been trying to establish: the problem of divine decree was already being argued over and discussed from the earliest period of Islam, before Maʿbad al-Juhanī, Ghaylān al-Dimashqī, and Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Ordinary Muslims already felt a need to decide where they stood on the issue. They raised it with the Prophet during his lifetime, with the Rightly Guided Caliphs after him, and with the Companions.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

The caliphs and Companions themselves did not all take the same position. We have seen this in the positions attributed to ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb and ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, and in the report about ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās, one of the greatest and most respected Companions, who is said by Ibn al-Murtaḍā to have “debated the Syrian supporters of compulsion and defeated their argument.” In other words, he defended human choice rather than compulsion.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

All this means that the problem of divine decree already existed whether or not Maʿbad al-Juhanī and Ghaylān al-Dimashqī had ever appeared, and whether or not they had raised the banner of human freedom in action.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
The conditions surrounding the problem were already capable of producing that position. They were also capable of producing the opposite position and of driving the two into conflict.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
That conflict would naturally lead to the emergence of two opposing schools on the question, just as it eventually did with the rise of the Muʿtazila and their opposite, the Ashʿarites.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Our final point is this: the historical setting shows that the problem had an objective reality of its own, independent of Maʿbad al-Juhanī and Ghaylān al-Dimashqī, their personal wishes, or their individual thinking.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Their decision to openly reject predestination and defend human freedom in action was therefore a response to an existing historical reality.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Of course, this does not mean that we deny the part played by personal choice and individual commitment in what they did. Otherwise, how could we explain their willingness to endure different forms of persecution for publicly defending a view that deeply angered the ruling authorities, until both men were eventually killed in acts of violence and revenge?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
What we have said so far raises a further question:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

What kind of conditions first produced Maʿbad al-Juhanī, and then Ghaylān al-Dimashqī, as open defenders of the view that human actions are not predetermined? What made them victims of that position? What then produced al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, who held the same view, and after him Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ, with whom this question and several others began to form the foundation of a rational school of Islamic doctrine? And what allowed that school—the Muʿtazila—to become a real turning point in the development of Arab thought toward philosophy?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

To answer this question, we turn again to Eastern and Western researchers. What we find is that most of them see only one side of the conditions that produced this development. And when some of them do notice another side, they do not place it where it actually belongs in historical reality.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Earlier, we discussed De Boer’s view of the origins of philosophical thought around Islamic beliefs. We may recall his claim that there are “scattered indications that some of the earliest Muslims who defended free choice had Christian teachers…”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

From this, he concludes that the earliest Muslim defenders of free choice had no real objective conditions within their own society that led them to discuss the idea of divine decree—or at least none worth considering. The explanation is reduced instead to the influence of Eastern Christians, who “almost all believed in free choice.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Other Western researchers deal with the question in much the same way.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Macdonald, for example, says that the problem of human freedom arises from a “philosophical necessity of the human mind.” That is his general explanation.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

When he turns to the concrete historical case, however, he argues that the doctrine of free will in Syria under the Umayyads arose under the influence of Christian ideas, especially the writings of John of Damascus. Those writings, he says, show that compulsion and freedom of the will were among the most important points of disagreement between Islam and Christianity.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Goldziher, meanwhile, quotes the researcher Kremer as saying that early Muslim scholars learned from Christian theologians in a way that caused them to question their previous belief in absolute eternal predestination.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Goldziher himself appears to see the main source of the Qadarite movement in the efforts of pious Muslims under the Umayyads to reconcile Qurʾanic passages that seemed to conflict over the relationship between God’s will and human will.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
These examples from Western scholarship explain the rise of debate over divine decree among Arab thinkers through one factor or another, but always from only one side.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Either they explain it entirely through the influence of Christian theology or some other outside source; or they appeal to a broad and abstract principle such as Macdonald’s “philosophical necessity of the human mind”; or they explain it as an attempt to reconcile Qurʾanic passages that appeared to contradict one another.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

What they do not ask is what social or political ground led early Muslims to make that attempt at reconciliation in the first place. Nor do they ask what led one group to defend predestination while another rejected it and defended human freedom of will and action.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Muslim historians themselves often explained the origins of the problem in the same way.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
They too tended to trace it entirely to the influence of Christian theology.
